question: Between 2013 and 2021, 33 712 cases of cancer in the EU were officially recognised as occupational, a term used for cancers that are generally caused by long-term exposure to carcinogenic factors present in the working environment.

According to the statistics for Member States, of the many types of occupational cancers, the most common were lung cancer and mesothelioma (which is linked to asbestos exposure), with almost 14 000 and 13 530 cases respectively. Bowel cancer is the third most prevalent (2 416 cases), followed by nasal and sinus cancer (930) and skin cancer (887).
However, the data we have often underestimate the extent of the issue because they do not factor in all the undiagnosed and unrecognised occupational cancers. In the light of these alarming data: 1.
What will the Commission do to protect the thousands of workers affected by occupational cancers?
In the interests of improving prevention and ensuring the swift recognition of occupational cancers, what steps need to be taken to develop better data collection methods?
answer: The Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan (1) is a political commitment of the Commission to fight against cancer, as part of a strong European Health Union.

As part of the implementation of this Plan, the Commission contributes to enhancing the prevention of occupational cancer by reducing the exposure of workers to hazardous substances via actions like the adoption of the EU Occupational safety and health (OSH) Strategic Framework (2) and proposals for amendments of Directive 2004/37/EC (3) and Directive 2009/148/EC (4).

Based on scientific research performed by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) (5), the Commission continuously sets new or revises the existing limit values for substances that are relevant for protection of workers exposed to carcinogens or mutagens. Recently, the Commission proposed the significant lowering of the limit value for asbestos and lead.
Further, the guide on asbestos will be updated and the Senior Labour Inspectors Committee (SLIC) will revise its asbestos guide and carry out awareness raising campaign on asbestos.

To develop better data collection methods, Eurostat currently conducts a pilot data collection on recognised occupational diseases from volunteering national authorities, the European Occupational Diseases Statistics (EODS) data collection. Eurostat publishes this experimental data on its website (6) where the EU Index of occupational diseases and country profiles are available.
This data collection includes information on the occupation of the victim (ISCO-08) (7) as well as on the economic activity sector of the institution the victim worked in (NACE Rev. 2) (8).
